extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers, compliance officers, and legal/regulatory counsel responsible for TILA/Regulation Z compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary interpreting Regulation Z sections on permitted late, returned-payment, and over-the-limit fees and on the form/location/formatting of tabular disclosures for credit card applications and solicitations. Focused on when fees may be imposed, fee-amount safe harbors, limits on multiple fees for a single event, the "smaller card issuer" threshold, and required disclosure formatting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on imposing an additional late payment fee for the same prior unpaid minimum payment (§1026.52(b)(2)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(ii) prohibits a card issuer from imposing an additional late payment fee if the prior required minimum payment that gave rise to a prior fee has not been received by a subsequent date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If an $8 late fee is imposed for missing the $20 minimum due March 25, the issuer may not impose another late fee later based solely on that same missed $20 payment (even if a later periodic statement shows a larger required minimum). But if the later periodic statement's required minimum is a new, separate required minimum and the previously-due amount has been satisfied per the statement, a new late fee may be imposed for failing to make the later required minimum. See illustrative fact patterns (March/April examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot impose multiple fees based on a single event or transaction (§1026.52(b)(2)(ii) - returned payment vs late fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2)(ii) prohibits imposing more than one fee that would be based on a single event or transaction—for example, both a returned-payment fee and a late payment fee arising from the same returned-check event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative scenarios: A check received and then returned for insufficient funds—issuer may impose either the late fee (if appropriate) or a returned-payment fee (e.g., $25 or $35 per safe harbors), but not both when they arise from the same returned-payment event. If different events occur (e.g., one payment returned and later no payment by the next due date), an additional late fee may be permitted later, subject to §1026.52(b)(2)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted timing for imposing a late payment fee (consistent with §1026.52(b)(1)(ii) and (b)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer may impose a late payment fee when the consumer has not made the required minimum periodic payment by the payment due date; timing examples show imposition on the day after the due date (e.g., impose an $8 fee on March 26 for a March 25 due date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate successive billing cycles: if a required minimum shown on a later statement includes earlier unpaid items, the issuer may impose a late fee for failure to make that later required minimum unless §1026.52(b)(2)(ii) prohibits imposing a second fee based on the earlier unpaid item. Several fact patterns illustrate when a late fee is and is not permitted based on payment and return timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor fee amounts referenced in examples (late fee, returned-payment fee, over-the-limit fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary examples reference specific safe-harbor fee amounts used in §1026.52 analyses (e.g., $8 late payment fee; returned-payment fee examples $25 or $35; over-the-limit fee examples $25 and $35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples show which fees may be imposed under the cited subsections in different fact patterns. They are illustrative of how the safe-harbor caps operate in practice and how different fees interact (e.g., returned-payment fee vs over-limit fee vs late fee), including prohibitions on imposing multiple fees for a single event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-the-limit fee imposition and recurrence rules (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(B) and §1026.56(j)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a consumer has affirmatively consented to transactions that exceed the credit limit, a card issuer may impose over-the-limit fees when the account balance becomes over the credit limit; such fees may be imposed if the balance remains more than the threshold amount on specified future dates, subject to §1026.56(j)(1) limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If balance exceeds the limit on March 31 and remains more than the specified threshold on April 26 and May 26, the issuer may impose over-the-limit fees ($35 examples) on those dates consistent with §1026.56(j)(1). After that, additional over-the-limit fees are not permitted unless another over-the-limit transaction occurs. Also, over-the-limit fees and late fees may both be imposed when they are based on different events (e.g., a late payment and a separate over-limit transaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Smaller Card Issuer' (fewer than one million open accounts for entire preceding calendar year) (§1026.52(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the definition of 'smaller card issuer,' a card issuer together with its affiliates must have fewer than one million open credit accounts for the entire preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the issuer exceeded one million open accounts for any part of the preceding calendar year, it is not a smaller card issuer for the next calendar year. An issuer only becomes a smaller card issuer when its open-account count (with affiliates) remains below one million for an entire preceding calendar year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition rule for becoming 'not smaller' when meeting/exceeding threshold in current year (§1026.52(b)(3)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an issuer had fewer than one million open accounts for the entire preceding calendar year but meets or exceeds one million open accounts in the current calendar year, the issuer will no longer meet the definition of 'smaller card issuer' as of 60 days after meeting or exceeding the threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of imposing a late fee under the safe harbor, the issuer may impose a late fee of no more than $8 as of the 60th day after meeting/exceeding the threshold. The transition is measured from the date the issuer meets/exceeds the account-count threshold in the current year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location and prominence of tabular disclosures on applications and solicitations (§1026.60(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabular disclosures required by §1026.60(b) must be prominently located on or with the application or solicitation (except for electronic exceptions). Disclosures are deemed prominent if on the same page as the application/reply form or if a clear and conspicuous reference indicates their location and that they contain rate, fee, and cost information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prominent placement: same page as an application or reply form; if elsewhere, the reply form must clearly and conspicuously reference where the disclosures are located and indicate their content. This ensures consumers can find rate/fee information in proximity to the application/solicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic tabular disclosures must be in close proximity; permitted methods (no read-confirmation required)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the table is provided electronically, it must be provided in close proximity to the application or solicitation. Issuers have flexibility in methods and are not required to confirm that the consumer has read the disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted methods include: (A) disclosures automatically appearing on the screen when the application/reply form appears; (B) disclosures located on the same web page as the application/reply form (even if not on initial screen) provided the form contains a clear and conspicuous reference to their location; (C) providing a link to the electronic disclosures on or with the application as long as consumers cannot bypass the disclosures before submitting; (D) locating disclosures on the same web page immediately preceding the submit button. The issuer need not require the consumer to scroll through disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-account disclosure formats
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tabular format is required, card issuers offering several types of accounts may disclose terms for multiple accounts in a single table or provide separate tables for each account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuers have discretion to group or separate account terms as long as the required information is presented in the tabular format where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion of inapplicable disclosures from the table (except grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures need only be given as applicable; card issuers may omit inapplicable headings and their corresponding boxes in the tabular disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if no foreign transaction fee applies, the 'Foreign transaction' heading and disclosure may be deleted, or the heading can remain with a disclosure showing 'none.' Exception: the grace period disclosure must be stated even if no grace period exists (the table must state that fact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting (bold) requirements for APRs and maximum fee limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Any maximum limits on fee amounts must be disclosed in bold text; other APRs or fee amounts disclosed in the table may not be in bold (with specified exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples G-10(B) and G-10(C) show guidance for bolding required items. Examples: the maximum limit of $8 for a late payment fee (when applicable) must be bolded; a cash advance fee with a maximum of $100 must have the $100 bolded. Other annual percentage rates or fee amounts should not be bolded unless they are maximum limits required to be highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic fees: display and bolding rules for periodic vs annualized amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Any periodic fee disclosed that is not an annualized amount must not be disclosed in bold; the corresponding annualized amount must be disclosed in bold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a $10 monthly maintenance fee should be shown as $10 (not bold) and also shown as $120 annualized (with the $120 bolded). If an annual fee must be disclosed, that annual fee amount itself must be bolded in the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of disclosures depends on access method (electronic versus paper) and location of consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: If a consumer accesses an application or solicitation electronically (e.g., online at home), the issuer must provide the disclosures in electronic form on or with the application or solicitation. If the consumer is physically present at the issuer's office and accesses the application electronically (via terminal/kiosk), the issuer may provide disclosures in either electronic or paper form, provided timing and delivery requirements ('on or with') are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the issuer mailed paper disclosures instead of providing them electronically to a remote online applicant, the timing/delivery requirement to provide disclosures 'on or with' the application would not be satisfied. When using in-person terminals/kiosks, issuers may choose paper or electronic so long as disclosures are timely and delivered on/with the application/solicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and substantial similarity to appendix G (§1026.60(a)(2)(i) and §1026.5(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.60(a)(2)(i) requires that the headings, content, and format of the tabular disclosures be substantially similar to the applicable tables in appendix G, though they need not be identical; terminology requirements in §1026.5(a)(2) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuers should follow the appendix G samples for headings and order, but may adapt formatting or terminology consistent with §1026.5(a)(2) provided the disclosures remain substantially similar and meet consumer understanding requirements.
